title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) in Adults
clinicalScenario: Outline only. Planned scope: Recognition and severity, fluids, fixed-rate insulin, potassium replacement, glucose and ketone monitoring, precipitant search, transition to subcutaneous insulin. Candidate sources to verify: JBDS-IP management of DKA in adults; ADA/EASD hyperglycaemic crises consensus.

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult (over 18 years) Emergency Department (ED) recognition and first 24 hours of treatment of Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA), based on the Joint British Diabetes Societies (JBDS) 2023 guideline, with the Saudi Ministry of Health (MOH) diabetes emergencies protocol and a review of the 2024 international consensus shown side by side where they differ.
findings: Full protocol rebuilt from the source dossier opened on 2026-10-21; exact source locations are recorded in each investigation and medicine row.
The original outline remains preserved; this additive version is non-current and pending clinical review.
unverifiedSections: Normal reference ranges are typical adult values, not taken from the cited guidelines; ranges differ between laboratories.
Symptoms, examination signs, differentials and the precipitant list are standard clinical content and were not extracted line by line from the opened sources.
The 2024 consensus was read through a 2025 review article, not the primary report (Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257–1275); numbers in the comparison column need checking against the primary report.

The Saudi MOH protocol is undated (cites 2015–2016 sources) and its potassium table layout is ambiguous in the opened text; the Saudi Diabetes Clinical Practice Guidelines DKA section (pp. 71–75) could not be opened.
JBDS prints the insulin volume as both 50 mL (Box 1) and 49.5 mL (p. 14); the potassium threshold below 3.5 mmol/L gives no replacement rate; page numbers were inferred from extracted footers.
Registration with the Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) was not checked for any drug.
The preferred insulin transition method (JBDS 30 minutes after subcutaneous short-acting insulin versus the 2024 consensus basal insulin 1–2 hours before stopping) is not settled between the sources.
At 40 mmol/L potassium chloride in a litre run over 2 hours the rate is 20 mmol/hour (derived); JBDS does not state a maximum potassium rate or central-line requirement.
The low-dose potassium row for potassium below 3.5 mmol/L borrows the hypokalaemia level rule from a Gloucestershire guideline past its review date; JBDS gives only 'senior review'.
The bicarbonate dose (JBDS recommends against routine use) and magnesium replacement are not given in the opened JBDS text.
JBDS page numbers are inferred from extracted page markers.

The VRIII scale table comes from a 2013 NHS trust chart (the first value column was unlabelled in the extract and is taken as Scale 1 from the total-daily-dose rule); the JBDS 2014 guideline table of units per hour was not readable. Check the Scale 1 column against the printed chart.

The Glasgow VRIII guideline uses one rate table (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 units/hour) and excludes DKA; it is lapsed (review due 1 November 2021). Its fluid rate is 100 mL/hour; JBDS gives 125 mL/hour and this protocol uses 125 mL/hour. A 2013 chart gives 5% glucose with 40 mmol potassium in 1 L at 100 mL/hour for potassium below 4.9 mmol/L.
The step down one scale for glucose 4–6 mmol/L on 2 readings is derived from the chart; JBDS states only to reduce the rate or raise glucose to 10%.
The weight multiplier or stable-phase calculation for the starting subcutaneous dose is not given in the opened JBDS summary.

The enoxaparin dose is from the manufacturer's international package insert (Sanofi India, CCDS version 14), not the Saudi SFDA label; the 20 mg renal dose applies below 30 mL/min creatinine clearance and the insert gives no separate lower band.

Renal, hepatic and age adjustments for the drugs added in this revision are from manufacturer labels (UK Summary of Product Characteristics, US prescribing information and a New Zealand data sheet), not from Saudi Food and Drug Authority labels.

pathophysiology.summary: Absolute or relative insulin deficiency with raised counter-regulatory hormones produces hyperglycaemia, ketone production and acidosis.
keyMechanisms: Insulin deficiency increases glucose release from the liver and breaks down fat into free fatty acids.
Free fatty acids are converted to ketone bodies (beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate), which cause a metabolic acidosis.
High glucose causes an osmotic diuresis, which produces dehydration and loss of sodium and potassium.
Acidosis moves potassium out of cells, so the measured potassium can look normal or high while total body potassium is low.
Sodium-Glucose Co-Transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors can cause DKA with only a mildly raised or normal glucose (euglycaemic DKA).

symptoms: Thirst, passing large volumes of urine, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain.
Weakness, drowsiness or confusion in severe cases.
physicalSigns: Dehydration with tachycardia and low blood pressure.
Deep, rapid breathing (Kussmaul breathing) and ketotic breath.
Reduced conscious level in severe cases.
redFlags: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score below 12 or an abnormal Alert, Voice, Pain, Unresponsive (AVPU) score.
Serum potassium below 3.5 mmol/L on admission needs senior review and extra potassium.
precipitants: Infection, missed or insufficient insulin, and new-onset type 1 diabetes.
Acute illness such as myocardial infarction or pancreatitis.
SGLT2 inhibitor treatment, which can cause euglycaemic DKA.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Glucose very high with osmolality of 320 mOsm/kg or more and little or no ketosis
Alcohol history with a normal or low glucose
Ketones present but pH and bicarbonate are not in the DKA range

clinicalManagement.title: Immediate
actions: Confirm all three diagnostic criteria. Start the clock (T=0) when intravenous (IV) fluids begin.
No IV access: ask for critical care help immediately.
SBP 90 mmHg or above: give 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over the first 60 minutes.
SBP below 90 mmHg: give 0.9% sodium chloride 500 mL over 10–15 minutes and repeat while waiting for senior input; once SBP is above 90 mmHg give 1 L over the next 60 minutes.
Start Fixed-Rate Intravenous Insulin Infusion (FRIII) at 0.1 units/kg/hour using estimated weight at T=0.
If a long-acting analogue (glargine, detemir or degludec) is normally taken, continue it at the usual dose and time.
Give an intramuscular (IM) insulin dose of 0.1 units/kg only if there is a delay in setting up the infusion.
Check potassium before adding it to fluids (see Medicines).
Measure capillary glucose and ketones hourly; vital signs and National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2) hourly after the first hour; record fluid balance with a minimum urine output of 0.5 mL/kg/hour.
Stop any SGLT2 inhibitor, complete a Yellow Card report and treat euglycaemic DKA in exactly the same way.

clinicalManagement.title: Ongoing
actions: Aim for a ketone fall of 0.5 mmol/L per hour, a bicarbonate rise of 3.0 mmol/L per hour and a glucose fall of 3.0 mmol/L per hour.
When glucose falls below 14 mmol/L, add 10% glucose at 125 mL/hour and consider reducing insulin to 0.05 units/kg/hour.
Continue 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L with potassium over 2 hours, 2 hours, 4 hours, 4 hours, then 6 hours. Reassess cardiovascular status at 12 hours; more fluid may be needed.
Use more cautious fluid replacement in people aged 18–25 years, older adults, pregnancy and heart or renal failure.
Do not give bicarbonate routinely.
Give prophylactic Low Molecular Weight Heparin (LMWH): enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously once daily (20 mg once daily if creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min).

At 6 hours check venous pH, bicarbonate, potassium, ketones and glucose. If DKA has not resolved, check the pump is working and connected and that the correct insulin volume is loaded, then review the infusion.
DKA is resolved when ketones are below 0.6 mmol/L and venous pH is above 7.3. Do not use bicarbonate to judge resolution.

Keep the insulin infusion running until the person is eating and drinking normally. If ketones have cleared (below 0.6 mmol/L, venous pH above 7.3) but the person is not eating, change to a Variable-Rate Intravenous Insulin Infusion (VRIII): choose the scale from usual total daily insulin, add the glucose and potassium fluid and follow the VRIII branches in Medicines.
VRIII target glucose is 6.0–10.0 mmol/L; check capillary glucose hourly while unstable; treat glucose below 4.0 mmol/L with the VRIII hypoglycaemia branch and restart the infusion within 20 minutes.
Stop VRIII only after subcutaneous insulin with background insulin has been given (see the VRIII stop and transition branch).

Change to subcutaneous insulin only when ketones are below 0.6 mmol/L, pH is above 7.3 and the person is eating and drinking. Do not stop the infusion until 30 minutes after subcutaneous short-acting insulin is given.

clinicalManagement.title: Escalation
actions: Severe DKA markers: ketones above 6.0 mmol/L, bicarbonate below 5.0 mmol/L, pH below 7.0, or GCS below 12 or abnormal AVPU. Involve senior and critical care teams.
SBP below 90 mmHg: consider critical care and senior input; consider other causes such as heart failure or sepsis.
Not improving against the ketone, bicarbonate and glucose targets: seek senior advice.
Watch for fluid overload and cerebral oedema; consider High Dependency Unit (HDU) care and a central line in high-risk groups.
Refer to the Diabetes Specialist Team (DST) within one working day of admission.

regimens.indication: Switch off ketone production and lower glucose
regimens.genericName: Human soluble insulin 1 unit/mL infusion (50 units in 50 mL 0.9% sodium chloride)
regimens.dose: Fixed-rate infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour of estimated weight. Rate in units/hour by weight: 40–49 kg = 4; 50–59 = 5; 60–69 = 6; 70–79 = 7; 80–89 = 8; 90–99 = 9; 100–109 = 10; 110–119 = 11; 120–130 = 12; 130–139 = 13; 140–150 = 14; over 150 kg = 15 (higher doses on Diabetes Specialist Team advice). No priming bolus. Intramuscular 0.1 units/kg only if the infusion is delayed. If after one hour ketones have fallen by less than 0.5 mmol/L/hour, bicarbonate has risen by less than 3 mmol/L/hour, or glucose has fallen by less than 3 mmol/L/hour, first check the pump is working, connected and loaded, then increase the rate by 1 unit/hour each hour
regimens.route: Preparation: draw 50 units of human soluble insulin (Actrapid, Humulin S) and make up to 50 mL with 0.9% sodium chloride in a syringe (JBDS p. 14 prints 49.5 mL of diluent) = 1 unit/mL; a ready-made solution is recommended. IV infusion by syringe pump. The insulin may share a line with the fluid only through a Y-connector with a one-way anti-siphon valve on a large-bore cannula
regimens.duration: Continue until ketones are below 0.6 mmol/L, venous pH is above 7.3 and the person is eating and drinking
adjustments: Renal impairment, hepatic impairment and older age can reduce insulin requirements: check glucose more often and adjust the dose individually
monitoring: Hourly capillary glucose and ketones
bicarbonate and potassium at 60 minutes, 2 hours then 2-hourly
continuous cardiac monitoring in severe DKA
contraindications: Hypokalaemia (potassium below 3.5 mmol/L): senior review before insulin is given
hypoglycaemia

learningObjectives: Recognise DKA using all three criteria and grade severity.
Start fluids and a fixed-rate insulin infusion promptly and manage potassium safely.
Know when to escalate and when DKA has resolved.
pitfalls: Stopping insulin when glucose normalises while ketones are still raised.
Using bicarbonate to judge resolution instead of ketones and pH.
Missing hypokalaemia (below 3.5 mmol/L) before insulin has taken effect.
Giving fast fluids to young adults aged 18–25 years, older adults, pregnant patients or those with heart or renal failure without senior review.
keyPoints: All three criteria (glucose, ketones, acidosis) must be present; euglycaemic DKA exists on SGLT2 inhibitors.
Fluids and fixed-rate insulin start together at T=0.
Keep insulin running with glucose until the person is eating and drinking.

patientEducation: Written sick-day rules and when to seek help.
Home ketone meters should be the default.
lifestyleAndDiet: Regular glucose and ketone monitoring and carbohydrate-aware eating, guided by the diabetes team.
mdtReferrals: Diabetes Specialist Team within one working day; critical care for severe DKA or no IV access.
dischargeCriteria: Ketones below 0.6 mmol/L, venous pH above 7.3, eating and drinking normally and converted to subcutaneous insulin.
Newly diagnosed diabetes: seen by the specialist team before discharge.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Refer to the DST within one working day of admission and review within 24 hours. Discharge with a written care plan copied to the General Practitioner (GP) and an out-of-hours contact number.
